What is this? You write with it in your notebook.

options.feedback: Incorrect. An eraser is used to clean mistakes.
Incorrect. A ruler is used to measure or draw straight lines.
Correct! You write with a pencil.
Incorrect. A backpack is used to carry things.

questions.explanation:
A pencil (lápiz) is an object used for writing or drawing. Other writing tools include pen (bolígrafo) and marker (marcador).

---

questions.statement: What do you use to **erase** pencil marks?

options.feedback: Incorrect. Scissors are used to cut.
Correct! An eraser (borrador) removes pencil marks.
Incorrect. A ruler is used for measuring.
Incorrect. A sharpener is used to sharpen pencils.

questions.explanation:
An eraser (borrador) is used to remove pencil marks from paper. In British English it is also called a "rubber".

---

questions.statement: Look at the picture. The teacher writes on the ________.

options.feedback: Incorrect. A desk is where students sit.
Incorrect. A chair is for sitting.
Correct! The teacher writes on the board (tablero).
Incorrect. The door is for entering and leaving.

questions.explanation:
The board (tablero) is what the teacher writes on in class. It can be a whiteboard (tablero blanco) or a blackboard (tablero negro/tradicional).

---

questions.statement: You put your books and notebooks inside a ____________.

options.feedback: Incorrect. A table is furniture, not for carrying things.
Incorrect. A window is part of the wall.
Correct! A backpack (mochila) carries your school supplies.
Incorrect. A clock shows the time.

questions.explanation:
A backpack (mochila) is a bag that students use to carry their books, notebooks, pencils and other school supplies to and from school.

---

questions.statement: The teacher says: "Please open your ____________ to page 10."

options.feedback: Incorrect. A pencil case holds pencils, not pages.
Correct! You open a book to read a page.
Incorrect. A ruler does not have pages.
Incorrect. You can't open a chair.

questions.explanation:
"Open your book" (abre tu libro) is a common classroom instruction. Students also hear "Close your book" (cierra tu libro) and "Turn to page..." (ve a la página...).

---

questions.statement: Mateo wants to borrow a pencil sharpener. What does he say?

options.feedback: Incorrect. That means he has one, not that he needs to borrow.
Incorrect. He is describing it, not asking.
Correct! This is the polite way to borrow something.
Incorrect. That is identifying the object, not asking.

questions.explanation:
To borrow something in English, we say "Can I borrow your [object]?" (¿Puedo tomar prestado tu...?). It is polite to ask before using someone else's things.

---

questions.statement:
The teacher says: "Take out your scissors and glue. We are going to make a craft."

What materials do the students need?

options.feedback: Incorrect. The teacher didn't mention those.
Correct! The teacher asked for scissors (tijeras) and glue (pegamento).
Incorrect. Those are for writing, not crafts.
Incorrect. Those are for measuring and sharpening.

questions.explanation:
"Take out your scissors and glue" means "saca tus tijeras y pegamento". Understanding classroom instructions is an important part of learning English in school.

---

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: The students sit on their ___________ and write on their ___________.

options.feedback: Correct! Students sit on chairs and write on desks.
Incorrect. You sit on chairs, not desks.
Incorrect. Students don't sit on boards.
Incorrect. Students usually don't sit on the floor in class.

questions.explanation:
In a classroom, students sit on chairs (sillas) and work at their desks (escritorios/pupitres). Desks usually have a flat surface for writing.

---

questions.statement: Read the classroom objects and choose the one that is NOT usually found in a pencil case:

options.feedback: Incorrect. Pencils are commonly kept in a pencil case.
Incorrect. Erasers are small and fit in a pencil case.
Correct! Scissors are larger and usually not kept in a pencil case.
Incorrect. Sharpeners are small and fit in a pencil case.

questions.explanation:
A pencil case (estuche) typically holds small items: pencils, pens, erasers, sharpeners, and crayons. Scissors (tijeras) are larger and usually kept separately.

---

questions.statement:
Look at the picture description. The teacher points to different objects and says:

1. "This is a book."
2. "This is a ruler."
3. "This is a door."
4. "This is a pencil."

Which one is NOT a school supply?

options.feedback: Incorrect. A book is a school supply.
Incorrect. A ruler is a school supply.
Correct! A door is part of the classroom, not a school supply.
Incorrect. A pencil is a school supply.

questions.explanation:
School supplies (útiles escolares) are objects used for learning: books, pencils, rulers, erasers, notebooks, etc. A door (puerta) is part of the classroom building, not a school supply.

---

questions.statement: What color is the sky on a clear day?

options.feedback: Incorrect. The sky is not red on a clear day.
Correct! The sky is blue on a clear day.
Incorrect. Grass is green, not the sky.
Incorrect. The sun is yellow, not the sky.

questions.explanation:
Blue (azul) is the color of the sky and the ocean. "Blue" is one of the most common color words in English.

---

questions.statement: How do you say the number **15** in English?
questions.explanation:
Numbers 13-19 end in "-teen": thirteen (13), fourteen (14), fifteen (15), sixteen (16), seventeen (17), eighteen (18), nineteen (19).

---

questions.statement: What color do you get when you mix **blue** and **yellow**?
questions.explanation:
Color mixing: Blue + Yellow = Green. This is basic color theory. Other mixes: Red + Yellow = Orange, Blue + Red = Purple.

---

Counting in English: ... twenty-seven (27), twenty-eight (28), twenty-nine (29), thirty (30). Numbers 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 are called twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety.

---

questions.statement: Camila has 3 red apples and 2 green apples. How many apples does she have in total?
questions.explanation:
To count total items: add the quantities. 3 (three) red apples + 2 (two) green apples = 5 (five) apples. Numbers can be used to count and add.

---

questions.statement:
Look at the description: "The Colombian flag has three colors: yellow, blue and red."

Which color is **not** mentioned?

options.feedback: Correct! Green is not in the Colombian flag.

questions.explanation:
The Colombian flag has three horizontal stripes: yellow (amarillo) at the top, blue (azul) in the middle, and red (rojo) at the bottom. Green (verde) is not in the flag.

---

questions.statement: The teacher asks: "How many students are in this class?" There are 12 boys and 11 girls. What is the answer?
questions.explanation:
Twelve (12) + eleven (11) = twenty-three (23). Learning to combine numbers in English is important for real-life situations like counting people in a class.

---

questions.statement:
Match the object with its color: **The sun is __________, grass is __________, and an elephant is __________.**

Which option completes the sentence correctly?

options.feedback: Correct! Sun = yellow, grass = green, elephant = gray.
Incorrect. The sun is not red.

questions.explanation:
Common color associations: sun = yellow (amarillo), grass = green (verde), elephant = gray (gris), sky = blue (azul), tomato = red (rojo).

---

questions.statement:
Santiago says: "I have forty-five marbles. I give fifteen to my friend."

How many marbles does Santiago have now? Write the answer in words.
questions.explanation:
Forty-five (45) minus fifteen (15) equals thirty (30). In English, subtraction is expressed as "minus" or "take away".

---

questions.statement:
Read the problem:

"There are ten red flowers, twenty yellow flowers, and fifteen pink flowers in the garden."

What is the total number of flowers? Choose the correct answer **in English words**.
questions.explanation:
Ten (10) + twenty (20) = thirty (30). Thirty (30) + fifteen (15) = forty-five (45). Practice adding numbers in English helps with both math and language skills.

---

questions.statement: My friend Sofia is very ________. She always shares her toys and helps everyone.
questions.context: Talking about your best friend in school.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Mean" is the opposite of sharing and helping. Sofia is the opposite of mean.
Correct. "Kind" describes a person who is friendly, generous, and considerate, like Sofia.
Incorrect. "Angry" describes a feeling of displeasure, but the sentence describes a permanent positive personality trait.
Incorrect. "Tall" describes physical height, but the sentence is about Sofia's behavior (sharing and helping).

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates the use of personality adjectives in context. The correct answer "kind" matches the description of sharing and helping. Common errors include choosing opposites or adjectives that describe physical appearance instead of personality.

---

questions.statement: Look at my new backpack! It is ________ and ________. I love the color of the sky!
questions.context: Describing a new backpack.

options.feedback: Incorrect. The context mentions "the color of the sky," which is blue, not red.
Correct. "Blue" matches the sky color, and "big" is a common adjective for a backpack.
Incorrect. "Old" contradicts "new backpack," and green is not the color of the sky.
Incorrect. "Thin" is not a typical description for a full backpack, and yellow is not the color of the sky.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates vocabulary related to colors and sizes. The student must use context clues ("new", "color of the sky") to select the appropriate adjectives. Errors usually stem from ignoring the context clues.

---

questions.statement: The elephant is ________, but the mouse is ________.
questions.context: Describing animals at the Santa Fe Zoo in Medellin.

options.feedback: Incorrect. While elephants aren't super fast, the main contrast between an elephant and a mouse is their size.
Correct. "Huge" describes the very large size of an elephant, and "tiny" describes the very small size of a mouse.
Incorrect. Elephants are usually grey and mice are grey or brown; these colors are not correct for these animals.
Incorrect. These are emotions, and the sentence is comparing the physical nature of these two animals.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates the use of antonyms (opposites) related to size. "Huge" and "tiny" provide the best contrast for these animals. Common errors include choosing irrelevant adjectives or incorrect colors.

---

questions.statement: My sister has ________ ________ hair, like a princess.
questions.context: Describing hair.

options.feedback: Incorrect. While possible, "princesses" in stories are traditionally described with long, often golden or bright hair.
Correct. This combination fits the traditional "princess" description often used in children's literature and movies.
Incorrect. Green is not a natural hair color; it doesn't fit a standard description.
Incorrect. Hair cannot be "square" in shape, and purple is not a natural hair color.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates the order of adjectives and vocabulary for hair description. "Long" (length) and "blonde" (color) are standard descriptions. Errors involve using unnatural colors or impossible shapes.

---

questions.statement: A lemon is usually ________ and it tastes ________.
questions.context: Describing a fruit from the market.

options.feedback: Incorrect. An orange is orange and sweet, but a lemon has a different color and taste.
Correct. Lemons are yellow on the outside and have a sour (acidic) taste.
Incorrect. This describes a chili pepper, not a lemon.
Incorrect. No common lemon is purple or salty.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates vocabulary for colors and tastes. The student must associate physical properties with the specific object "lemon". Errors are usually due to confusing different fruits or taste adjectives.

---

questions.statement: My grandfather is ________, but he is very ________. He plays football with me!
questions.context: Describing people in the family.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Grandfathers are usually old, not young. If he was tired, he wouldn't play football.
Correct. "Old" is typical for a grandfather, and "energetic" explains why he can play football despite his age.
Incorrect. "New" is for objects, not for people like a grandfather.
Incorrect. These adjectives don't contrast well with the fact that he plays football.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates the use of adjectives with a logical contrast (but). The student must find a pair that makes sense with the role of "grandfather" and the action of "playing football". Errors involve using adjectives that don't apply to humans.

---

questions.statement: Today in Bogota, the weather is ________. I need my umbrella and a jacket!
questions.context: Describing the weather in Bogota.

options.feedback: Incorrect. If it's sunny and hot, you don't need an umbrella for rain or a jacket for cold.
Correct. You need an umbrella when it's rainy and a jacket when it's cold. This fits Bogota's weather.
Incorrect. These conditions don't require an umbrella or a warm jacket.
Incorrect. This describes a sunny day, which contradicts the need for an umbrella.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates weather vocabulary through logical deduction. The "umbrella" and "jacket" are key clues for "rainy" and "cold". Errors come from failing to connect the objects to the weather condition.

---

questions.statement: The English exam was very ________. I am ________ because I got a 10!
questions.context: Describing feelings after a test.

options.feedback: Incorrect. If you get a 10 (the best grade), you wouldn't be sad.
Correct. If the exam was easy, getting a 10 makes sense, and you would feel happy.
Incorrect. Getting a 10 is a positive thing; being angry doesn't match the result.
Incorrect. "Boring" is a feeling about interest, not a feeling about a successful result.

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates adjectives for difficulty and emotions. The high grade (10) implies the exam was manageable and the student is satisfied. Errors are usually due to mismatched logic between the result and the emotion.

---

questions.statement: My monster has three ________ eyes and a ________ mouth. It is scary!
questions.context: Describing a monster in a drawing.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Small mouths are usually not associated with being "scary" monsters.
Correct. Huge mouths are typical for "scary" monsters in children's drawings.
Incorrect. "Beautiful" and "pink" are not typical adjectives for something described as "scary".
Incorrect. "Sweet" and "nice" are the opposite of "scary".

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates the use of descriptive adjectives for fantasy creatures. The word "scary" is the clue to choose "huge" and "round" (or other intimidating features). Errors occur when choosing positive adjectives for a negative context.

---

questions.statement: My bedroom is very ________. My toys are on the floor and my bed is not made.
questions.context: Describing a room.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Clean" means everything is in its place, but the toys are on the floor.
Incorrect. "Tidy" is a synonym for organized. Toys on the floor mean the room is not tidy.
Correct. "Messy" describes a room with things out of place, like toys on the floor and an unmade bed.
Incorrect. If there are toys and a bed, the room is not empty.

questions.explanation: This question evaluates vocabulary for domestic descriptions. "Messy" is the correct adjective for the lack of order described. Errors usually come from confusing "messy" with its opposites like "clean" or "tidy".

options.feedback: Correct! "Mom" is another word for mother.

questions.explanation:
Mother and mom both mean "mamá" or "madre" in Spanish. "Mom" is more informal and commonly used in daily conversation.

---

options.feedback: Correct! Your father's brother is your uncle (tío).

questions.explanation:
Family relationships: father's brother = uncle (tío), mother's brother = uncle too. Your uncle's children are your cousins (primos).

---

options.feedback: Incorrect. Cousins are children of your aunts/uncles.
Correct! The parents of your parents are your grandparents (abuelos).
Incorrect. Siblings are brothers and sisters.
Incorrect. Neighbors are people who live near you.

questions.explanation:
Grandparents (abuelos) are the parents of your parents. Your mother's parents and father's parents are both your grandparents. Grandfather = abuelo, Grandmother = abuela.

---

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Siblings" includes both brothers and sisters.
Correct! Siblings refers to all brothers and sisters.

questions.explanation:
"Siblings" (hermanos) is a general term that includes both brothers (hermanos varones) and sisters (hermanas). If you have one brother and one sister, you have two siblings.

---

questions.statement:
Valentina says: "My mother's name is María. My father's name is José. I have one brother, Andrés."

How many people are in Valentina's immediate family?

options.feedback: Incorrect. She mentioned more than two.
Incorrect. She mentioned four people total.
Correct! Valentina, her mother, her father, and her brother = 4 people.
Incorrect. She only mentioned four people.

questions.explanation:
Valentina's immediate family (familia nuclear) includes: herself (Valentina), her mother (María), her father (José), and her brother (Andrés). That is four people.

---

questions.statement:
Look at the sentence: "This is my _________, Laura. She is my father's sister."

Which word completes the sentence?

options.feedback: Correct! Your father's sister is your aunt (tía).
Incorrect. A cousin is not the parent's sister.

questions.explanation:
Aunt (tía) can be: your father's sister, your mother's sister, or your uncle's wife. Uncle (tío) is the male equivalent.

---

questions.statement: Carlos is describing his family. Which sentence is CORRECT?

options.feedback: Incorrect. The verb should be "have", not "has" with "I".
Incorrect. It should be "My sister's name" (possessive).
Correct! The possessive form uses an apostrophe + s.

questions.explanation:
To show possession in English, we use 's (apóstrofe + s). "My sister's name" = "el nombre de mi hermana". Also remember: "I have" not "I has".

---

questions.statement:
Read the family tree:
- Tom and Ana are married.
- Tom and Ana have two children: a boy named Luke and a girl named Emma.

Who is Emma to Tom?

options.feedback: Correct! Emma is the daughter of Tom.
Incorrect. Tom is Emma's father, not brother.

questions.explanation:
Family relationships from a family tree: Tom is the father, Ana is the mother. Luke is their son (hijo) and Emma is their daughter (hija).

---

questions.statement: Camila says: "My mother's brother is my uncle. His daughter is my ________."

options.feedback: Incorrect. The daughter of your uncle is not your sister.
Incorrect. She is younger than your mother, so not aunt.
Correct! The daughter of your uncle is your cousin (prima).
Incorrect. Niece is your sibling's daughter.

questions.explanation:
Your uncle's children are your cousins (primos). Male cousin = primo, female cousin = prima. Your mother's brother = uncle, and his daughter = your cousin.

---

questions.statement:
Read this description and choose the correct family diagram:

"I have a big family. I live with my mom, dad, and little brother. My grandparents live next door. My aunt and uncle visit every Sunday with my two cousins."

How many people are in the speaker's **immediate family** (who live with them)?

options.feedback: Incorrect. The grandparents don't live with them.
Correct! The speaker + mom + dad + little brother = 4.
Incorrect. That's counting extended family too.
Incorrect. The speaker mentioned 4 immediate family members.

questions.explanation:
Immediate family (familia nuclear) = people who live together. Here: speaker, mom, dad, little brother = 4. Extended family (familia extendida) = grandparents, aunt, uncle, cousins.

---

options.feedback: Incorrect. You use ears to hear.
Correct! You see with your eyes (ojos).
Incorrect. You use your mouth to eat and speak.
Incorrect. You use your nose to smell.

questions.explanation:
Parts of the face and their functions: eyes (ojos) = see/ver, ears (orejas) = hear/oír, nose (nariz) = smell/oler, mouth (boca) = eat/comer and speak/hablar.

---

questions.statement: You have two of these at the end of your arms. You use them to hold things.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Feet are at the end of your legs.
Incorrect. Knees are in the middle of your legs.
Correct! You hold things with your hands (manos).
Incorrect. Shoulders connect arms to the body.

questions.explanation:
Hands (manos) are at the end of your arms. Each hand has five fingers (dedos). We use our hands to grab, hold, write, and touch things.

---

questions.statement: Your **head** is connected to your body by your ________.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Legs are at the bottom of your body.
Incorrect. Arms are on the sides of your body.
Correct! The neck (cuello) connects the head to the body.
Incorrect. The back is the rear part of your body.

questions.explanation:
The neck (cuello) is the part of the body that connects the head to the torso (tronco). It allows the head to turn and move.

---

questions.statement: You have ten of these on your feet. You use them to walk and balance.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Fingers are on your hands, not feet.
Correct! Toes (dedos de los pies) are on your feet.
Incorrect. Heels (talones) are the back part of your feet.
Incorrect. Ankles (tobillos) connect feet to legs.

questions.explanation:
Toes (dedos de los pies) are the digits on your feet. You have 10 toes (5 on each foot). Fingers (dedos de las manos) are on your hands. You also have 10 fingers.

---

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: "I ________ two arms and two legs."

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Has" is used with he/she/it, not "I".
Correct! "I have" is correct for describing body parts.
Incorrect. "I am" is used with adjectives, not possession.

questions.explanation:
"I have" (yo tengo) is used to describe the body parts you possess. "He/she has" (él/ella tiene) is used for other people. Example: "I have blue eyes. She has brown eyes."

---

questions.statement:
Read the description: "Pedro has a big mouth, small eyes, and long arms."

Which of these does Pedro **not** have described?

questions.statement:

First the nose, then the ears

Incorrect. The teacher gave two instructions.
Incorrect. The first instruction was to touch the nose.

questions.explanation:
Following instructions in English: "Touch your nose" = toca tu nariz. "Touch your ears" = toca tus orejas. It's important to follow the sequence of commands.

questions.statement:

Correct! 3 eyes + 1 mouth + 4 arms = 8 body parts.

questions.explanation:
Sofia describes: 3 eyes (tres ojos), 1 big mouth (una boca grande), and 4 arms (cuatro brazos). Total body parts mentioned: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8.

questions.statement:

Incorrect. Cats don't wear glasses or have hands.

questions.explanation:

options.text: She has long hair and green eyes.

options.feedback: Incorrect. In English, adjectives come before nouns.

options.text: She has a long hair and a green eyes.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Hair" and "eyes" are uncountable/plural, don't use "a".

questions.explanation:

questions.statement: How do you say **"Hola"** in English?

questions.statement: What do you say when you **meet someone for the first time**?

Incorrect. You say "I'm sorry" when you make a mistake.

questions.statement:

**Teacher:** What is your name?
**Student:** ________________

options.feedback: Incorrect. That answers age, not name.
Correct! The question asks for the name.
Incorrect. That answers where you are from.
Incorrect. That is not an answer to "What is your name?".

questions.explanation:
"What is your name?" pregunta por el nombre. La respuesta correcta es "My name is..." (Mi nombre es...) o "I am..." (Yo soy...).

---

questions.statement:

options.feedback: Correct! "How old are you?" asks about age.
Incorrect. That answers where you are from.
Incorrect. That answers what you do.

questions.explanation:
"How old are you?" pregunta por la edad. Se responde "I am [number] years old" (Tengo [número] años). Ejemplo: "I am ten years old."

---

questions.statement: Sofía is from Colombia. She wants to tell a new friend where she is from. What does she say?

Incorrect. "I like" means "me gusta", not origin.
Incorrect. The question is about her country, not city.

questions.explanation:
Para decir de dónde eres se usa "I am from [country/city]". Sofía diría "I am from Colombia". También puede decir "I am Colombian" para expresar su nacionalidad.

questions.statement: Mateo is 9 years old. He wants to write about himself. Which sentence is CORRECT?

options.feedback: Incorrect. The word order is wrong.

Incorrect. The expression is "I am nine years old".

questions.explanation:
En inglés, para decir la edad se usa "I am [number] years old". No se dice "I have [number] years" (como en español "tengo 9 años") ni se invierte el orden de las palabras.

**Pedro:** My name is Pedro. Nice to meet you.

questions.explanation:
Ana se presenta ("My name is Ana") y luego pregunta el nombre de Pedro. La pregunta correcta es "What is your name?" (¿Cuál es tu nombre?). Pedro responde con su nombre.

---

questions.statement:

**Student:** ________________

options.feedback: Incorrect. That answers "How are you?", not a name question.

options.text: My name is Carlos. Nice to meet you.
options.feedback: Correct! This is polite and appropriate for the situation.

options.text: Carlos is my name. I am nine.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The age is not asked here.
Incorrect. This is not an answer to "What is your name?".

questions.explanation:
Al ser presentado por un adulto (Mr. Smith), el estudiante debe responder con su nombre de forma educada: "My name is Carlos. Nice to meet you." Es importante ser cortés al conocer a alguien nuevo.

options.text: "Hi! I am Camila. I am from Bogotá. I am ten years old."

options.feedback: Incorrect. The name should come before the other information.
